subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Cytopathic effect (CPE) is the visible damage a virus causes to cultured cells, helping identify the virus. It reflects viral replication and cell death patterns, not the disease severity in patients.

sections.p: CPE is the observable change in cell morphology after viral infection in vitro. It is a key diagnostic clue in virology labs.
Viruses that produce distinct CPE include paramyxoviruses, coronaviruses, adenoviruses, and many others. The pattern depends on viral proteins that alter host cell membranes.
Viruses replicate inside host cells, using host machinery to produce new virions. In culture, the same cycle occurs, leading to visible CPE.
CPE itself is a laboratory phenomenon; the clinical disease depends on the virus. For example, measles virus causes rash and fever, not the CPE seen in culture.
Virus isolation in cell culture is followed by microscopic observation of CPE. Specific patterns guide further identification by immunofluorescence or PCR.
No therapy targets CPE directly; treatment focuses on the underlying virus. Antivirals, supportive care, and infection control measures are key.
b: Isolation and hygiene to prevent spread

sections.p: Remember that CPE is a laboratory sign, not a clinical one. Different viruses produce characteristic CPE patterns; use this to narrow differential diagnosis.
b: CPE patterns: syncytia (paramyxovirus), inclusion bodies (adenovirus), cell rounding (influenza).

faq.q: What does CPE tell us about the patient?
faq.a: It indicates the virus is replicating in vitro; it does not reflect disease severity or prognosis in the patient.

faq.q: Can CPE be seen in all viruses?
faq.a: No. Some viruses (e.g., HIV) do not produce obvious CPE in standard cell lines.

faq.q: Is CPE the same as cytopathic damage in tissues?
faq.a: No. Tissue damage in patients is often immune-mediated; CPE is direct viral effect on cultured cells.

exam: Explain how syncytia formation in cell culture helps identify a paramyxovirus.
Describe the steps to confirm a virus after observing CPE in a cell line.
Discuss why a virus that does not produce CPE in culture might still be clinically significant.
